title: Part 1, Chapter 44
paragraphs: In which the extraordinary adventures at the inn continue

Don Quixote was shouting so loudly, in fact, that the landlord threw open the gate of the inn in a hurry and came out alarmed, running to see who was making such a racket, and the people outside joined him. Maritornes, who had been woken by the same uproar and guessed what was going on, ran up to the loft and, without anyone noticing her, untied the halter that Don Quixote was hanging from. Down he dropped to the ground in full view of the landlord and the travelers, who came up and asked him what was wrong with him that he was yelling like that. Without answering a word, he pulled the rope off his wrist, got to his feet, leaped onto Rocinante, braced his shield on his arm, set his lance in position, and after riding a wide circuit around the plain came back at a half-gallop, declaring:
"Whoever claims that I was enchanted with good reason — provided my lady the Princess Micomicona gives me permission to do so — I call him a liar, I challenge him, and I defy him to single combat."

The newly arrived travelers were astonished at Don Quixote's words, but the landlord cleared up their confusion by telling them who he was and saying they shouldn't pay him any attention, since he was out of his mind. They then asked the landlord whether by any chance a boy of about fifteen had come to the inn, dressed like a mule driver and looking such and such a way — and the description they gave was of Doña Clara's lover. The landlord answered that there were so many people at the inn that he hadn't noticed the person they were asking about. But one of them, spotting the coach the Judge had arrived in, said, "He's here, no question — this is the coach he's been following. Let one of us stay at the gate and the rest go in to look for him. Actually, it would be a good idea for one of us to circle around the inn too, in case he tries to escape over the wall of the yard." "Agreed," said another; and while two of them went inside, one stayed at the gate and the other walked the perimeter of the inn. The landlord watched all this, unable to figure out why they were taking so many precautions, though he understood they were looking for the boy they had described to him.

By now it was broad daylight, and for that reason — and because of the noise Don Quixote had made — everyone was awake and up, especially Doña Clara and Dorothea, who had both slept badly that night: one out of agitation at having her lover so close, the other out of curiosity to see him. When Don Quixote saw that none of the four travelers paid him any attention or answered his challenge, he was furious — ready to die of indignation and rage. If he could have found anything in the rules of chivalry making it lawful for a knight-errant to take on or get involved in a new enterprise after he had pledged his word and faith not to commit himself to any until he had finished the one he was already bound to, he would have attacked the whole lot of them and forced them to answer whether they liked it or not. But considering that it would not be proper, or right, to begin any new venture until he had restored Micomicona to her kingdom, he had to hold his tongue and wait quietly to see how the travelers' business would play out. One of them found the boy they were looking for, sleeping beside a mule driver, with no idea that anyone was coming after him, much less that he would be found.
The man grabbed him by the arm and said, "This outfit really suits you, Señor Don Luis — and the bed I find you in certainly matches the luxury your mother raised you in."

The boy rubbed his sleepy eyes and stared for a moment at the man holding him, then recognized him as one of his father's servants. The shock left him so stunned that for a while he couldn't find a word to say, while the servant went on: "There's nothing for it now, Señor Don Luis, but to come quietly and go back home — unless you want my lord, your father, to depart for the next world, because nothing else can come of the grief your absence is causing him."
"But how did my father know I had taken this road, and in these clothes?" said Don Luis.

"It was a student you confided your plans to," the servant answered, "who revealed them, moved by pity at the distress he saw your father suffering when you went missing. So your father sent four of his servants out to find you, and here we all are at your service — happier than you can imagine that we'll be back so soon and able to return you to the eyes that long for you so much."
"That will be as I choose, or as heaven decides," Don Luis replied.
"What can you choose, or heaven decide," said the other, "except to agree to come back? Anything else is impossible."

The whole exchange between the two of them was overheard by the mule driver lying next to Don Luis, who got up and went to report what had happened to Don Fernando, Cardenio, and the others, who by now had gotten dressed. He told them how the man had addressed the boy as "Don," what words had passed between them, and how the man wanted him to go back to his father, which the boy refused to do. With this, and with what they already knew of the remarkable voice heaven had given him, they all became very eager to learn more precisely who he was — and even to help him if anyone tried to use force against him. So they hurried over to where he was still talking and arguing with his servant. At that moment Dorothea came out of her room with Doña Clara trembling behind her; calling Cardenio aside, she briefly told him the story of the singer and Doña Clara, while he in turn told her what had just happened — how his father's servants had come looking for him. But he didn't speak quietly enough, and Doña Clara overheard, which upset her so badly that if Dorothea hadn't rushed to hold her up, she would have collapsed to the ground. Cardenio then told Dorothea to take her back to her room, saying he would try to sort the whole thing out, and they did as he asked. By now all four men who had come after Don Luis were inside the inn and had surrounded him, pressing him to come back and console his father immediately, without a moment's delay. He answered that he could not possibly do so until he had settled a matter on which his life, his honor, and his heart all depended. The servants kept pressing him, insisting that they would absolutely not go back without him and that they would take him away whether he liked it or not.
"You will not do that," Don Luis replied, "unless you take me dead — though however you take me, it will be without life."

By this point the argument had drawn most of the people at the inn, especially Cardenio, Don Fernando, his companions, the Judge, the priest, the barber, and Don Quixote — who had decided there was no longer any need to stand guard over the castle. Cardenio, who already knew the young man's story, asked the men who wanted to take him away what their purpose was in trying to carry the boy off against his will.
"Our purpose," said one of the four, "is to save the life of his father, who is in danger of losing it because of this gentleman's disappearance."
At this Don Luis burst out, "There is no need to air my private affairs here. I am free; I will go back if I choose, and if not, none of you can force me."
"Reason will force you, sir," said the man, "and if it has no power over you, it has power over us — to make us do what we came here for, and what it is our duty to do."

"Let's hear what this whole business is about," said the Judge at this point. But the man, who knew him as a neighbor of theirs, answered, "Don't you recognize this gentleman, Señor Judge? He's the son of your neighbor — he's run away from his father's house in clothes far beneath his station, as your worship can see."

At this the Judge looked at him more closely and recognized him, and embracing him he said, "What foolishness is this, Señor Don Luis? What could possibly have driven you to come here like this, in clothes so unworthy of your position?"

Tears came to the young man's eyes, and he couldn't get out a word in reply to the Judge, who told the four servants not to worry — everything would be settled to everyone's satisfaction. Then, taking Don Luis by the hand, he drew him aside and asked him why he had come there.

But while he was questioning him, a loud commotion broke out at the gate of the inn. The cause was this: two guests who had spent the night there, seeing everyone preoccupied with finding out what the four men wanted, had decided to slip away without paying their bill. But the landlord, who minded his own business more closely than other people's, caught them on their way out the gate and demanded payment, cursing their dishonesty in language that provoked them to answer with their fists. They started laying into him so hard that the poor man had to scream and call for help. The landlady and her daughter could see no one more available to help than Don Quixote, and the daughter said to him, "Sir knight, by the strength God has given you, help my poor father — two wicked men are beating him to a pulp."

To which Don Quixote replied, very deliberately and calmly, "Fair maiden, your request comes at the wrong moment, for I am barred from involving myself in any adventure until I have brought to a happy conclusion the one my word has bound me to. But here is what I can do for you: run and tell your father to hold his ground as best he can in this battle and on no account to let himself be defeated, while I go and ask the Princess Micomicona's permission to rescue him from his distress. If she grants it, you can be sure I will get him out of it."
"Sinner that I am," exclaimed Maritornes, who was standing nearby, "before you get your permission my master will be in the next world."

"Allow me, señora, to obtain the permission I mentioned," Don Quixote answered, "and once I have it, it will hardly matter if he is in the next world, for I will rescue him from there despite anything that same world can do — or at the very least I will give you such revenge on those who sent him there that you will be more than reasonably satisfied." And without another word he went and knelt before Dorothea, begging her Highness, in the language of knight-errantry, to be so good as to grant him permission to aid and rescue the castellan of that castle, who now stood in grave peril. The princess granted it graciously, and he immediately braced his shield on his arm, drew his sword, and hurried to the inn gate, where the two guests were still roughing up the landlord. But the moment he got there he stopped short and stood still, even though Maritornes and the landlady asked him why he was hesitating to help their master and husband.

"I hesitate," said Don Quixote, "because it is not lawful for me to draw my sword against people of a squire's rank. Call my squire Sancho here for me — this defense and this vengeance are his affair and his business."

So matters stood at the inn gate, where fists and punches were flying back and forth, all to the landlord's serious damage and to the fury of Maritornes, the landlady, and her daughter, who were beside themselves at Don Quixote's cowardice and at the rough treatment their master, husband, and father was taking. But let us leave him there — he'll surely find someone to help him, and if not, let the man who attempts more than his strength allows suffer in silence — and let us step back fifty paces to see how Don Luis answered the Judge, whom we left questioning him privately about his reasons for traveling on foot and dressed so shabbily.
The young man, gripping his hand in a way that showed his heart was weighed down by some great sorrow, and weeping a flood of tears, answered:

"Señor, I have nothing more to tell you than this: from the moment when, by heaven's will and because we were near neighbors, I first saw Doña Clara, your daughter and my lady — from that instant I made her the mistress of my will, and if your will, my true lord and father, raises no objection, this very day she shall become my wife. For her I left my father's house, and for her I put on this disguise, to follow her wherever she might go, as the arrow seeks its target or the sailor the pole star. She knows nothing more of my feelings than what she may have gathered from sometimes seeing, at a distance, that my eyes were full of tears. You already know, señor, the wealth and noble birth of my parents, and that I am their only heir. If that is enough to persuade you to risk making me completely happy, accept me as your son right now. And if my father, with other plans of his own, should disapprove of this happiness I have found for myself — well, time has more power to alter and change things than human will does."

With that the lovesick young man fell silent, and the Judge, having heard him out, was astonished, perplexed, and taken aback — both by the manner and intelligence with which Don Luis had confessed what was in his heart, and by the position he himself was now in, not knowing what to do about something so sudden and unexpected. So the only answer he gave was to tell him to calm himself for the moment and to arrange with his servants not to take him back that day, so there would be time to think about what was best for everyone. Don Luis insisted on kissing his hands — bathed them in tears, in fact — in a way that would have moved a heart of marble, let alone the Judge's. Being a shrewd man, the Judge had already seen how advantageous this marriage would be for his daughter, though if it were possible he would have preferred it to happen with the consent of Don Luis's father, who, he knew, had his sights set on a title for his son.

By this time the guests had made peace with the landlord — thanks to persuasion and Don Quixote's fair words more than to any threats, they had paid him what he demanded — and Don Luis's servants were waiting for the conversation with the Judge to end and for their master's decision, when the devil, who never sleeps, arranged for the barber — the one from whom Don Quixote had taken Mambrino's helmet, and Sancho Panza the gear of his donkey in exchange for his own — to walk into the inn at that very moment. As this barber was leading his donkey to the stable, he noticed Sancho Panza fixing something or other on the pack-saddle, and the instant he saw it he recognized it, and boldly went for Sancho, shouting, "Aha, you thief, I've caught you! Hand over my basin and my pack-saddle and all the gear you robbed me of!"

Sancho, finding himself attacked so unexpectedly and hearing the insults being heaped on him, grabbed the pack-saddle with one hand and with the other gave the barber a punch that bathed his teeth in blood. The barber, however, was not about to let go of the prize he had seized in the pack-saddle; on the contrary, he raised such an outcry that everyone in the inn came running to find out what the noise and the quarrel were about. "Here, in the name of the king and of justice!" he cried. "This thief and highway robber wants to kill me for trying to recover my own property!"
"You're lying," said Sancho. "I'm no highway robber — my master Don Quixote won these spoils in fair war."

Don Quixote was standing nearby at the time, delighted to see his squire's toughness on both offense and defense, and from then on he considered him a man of real spirit. In his heart he resolved to dub him a knight at the first opportunity that came along, feeling certain that the order of chivalry would be well bestowed on him.

In the course of the argument, the barber said, among other things, "Gentlemen, this pack-saddle is mine as surely as I owe God a death. I know it as well as if I'd given birth to it, and my donkey is right there in the stable and won't let me lie — just try it on him, and if it doesn't fit him like a glove, call me a scoundrel. And what's more, the same day this was stolen from me, they also robbed me of a brand-new brass basin, never even used, that would fetch a crown any day of the week."

At this Don Quixote couldn't keep himself from answering. Stepping between the two of them and separating them, he set the pack-saddle on the ground, where it could stay in plain sight until the truth was established, and said, "Your worships can see clearly and plainly the error this worthy squire is laboring under when he calls a basin something that was, is, and always shall be the helmet of Mambrino, which I won from him in fair war and made myself master of by legitimate and lawful possession. With the pack-saddle I have nothing to do; but on that subject I can tell you that my squire Sancho asked my permission to strip the trappings from this defeated coward's steed and use them to outfit his own. I gave him permission, and he took them. As for how they were transformed from horse-trappings into a pack-saddle, I can offer no explanation except the usual one — that such transformations happen in the adventures of chivalry. To confirm all of this — run, Sancho my son, and bring here the helmet that this good fellow calls a basin."

"Good grief, master," said Sancho, "if we have no better proof of our case than what your worship is offering, then Mambrino's helmet is just as much a basin as this fellow's trappings are a pack-saddle."
"Do as I tell you," said Don Quixote. "It can't be that everything in this castle runs on enchantment."
Sancho hurried off to where the basin was and brought it back, and when Don Quixote saw it, he took it in his hands and said:

"Your worships can see what nerve this squire has, claiming that this is a basin and not the helmet I told you about. And I swear by the order of chivalry I profess that this helmet is the very same one I took from him, with nothing added to it and nothing taken away."

"There's no doubt about that," said Sancho, "because from the time my master won it until now, he's fought only one battle in it — the time he set those unlucky men in chains loose. And if it hadn't been for this basin-helmet, he wouldn't have come out of that one too well, because there was plenty of stone-throwing in that affair."
